https://www.capradio.org/articles/2026/0.text: Inside California Forever’s high-pressure push to fast-track a shipyard Thursday, August 20, 2026 | Sacramento, CA Cattle graze on land where California Forever plans to build its new city in Solano County on Feb. 16, 2024. The development would be located between Travis Air Force Base and Rio Vista. Loren Elliot/CalMatters By Yue Stella Yu and Kate Wolffe , CalMatters This story was originally published by CalMatters . Sign up for their newsletters. Last September, at their final meeting before the legislative session ended, Solano County supervisors were pressed to endorse state legislation — right away. Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office had blessed a legislative proposal to fast-track a new shipyard along the Northern California county’s waterfront, and supervisors needed to decide if they would support it. But the board had just received the draft language hours before, so, after a 15-minute break to read the documents and an hour of public commentary, Supervisor Wanda Williams asked whether she could suggest changes. “I don’t think we got time. We got 10 minutes,” said then-Board Chair Mitch Mashburn , gesturing toward the clock. The shipyard was a pitch by California Forever, the tech billionaire-backed brainchild of a Czech-born entrepreneur named Jan Sramek. Since it began quietly purchasing Solano County land in 2018, the company has spent $1 billion acquiring nearly 70,000 acres — more than 10% of the county. Initially, Sramek pitched the idea of building a dense, walkable city of 400,000 people with good-paying local jobs. Later, he added to the proposal a significant manufacturing hub and a state-of-the-art shipyard. From the start, local residents put up a fight: many were distrustful of the group’s secretive beginnings, antagonistic relationship with farmers , and possible risks the project posed to the environment. The supervisors’ vote followed two weeks of aggressive lobbying by California Forever representatives, who pressured county staff to support state legislation they had not seen, accused them of delaying the process and said they’d be responsible for the loss of 10,000 potential jobs and billions of dollars in revenue, according to email and text exchanges obtained by CalMatters. In the end, supervisors supported a last-minute bill they had barely read so they could at least have a say in the development they believed Sacramento might force down their throat within days. “As much as I have to throw up in my mouth a little bit and swallow that, and I’m sorry to use that analogy for everybody, I have to say that yes, I want us to be able to have a voice,” said Mashburn, before voting in favor. The records offer a glimpse into how California Forever has leveraged the prospect of economic development to pressure local officials into supporting its legislative agenda, often against a tight timeline. Now, in the final weeks of this year’s legislative session, California Forever is again pushing for quick action. Urgent legislation, again California Forever’s Director of Partnerships Michael Fortney defended last year’s urgency, saying that the region’s high unemployment rate — the highest in the Bay Area — and a series of departures of major employers such as Budweiser and Valero, “were not reasons to move slower.” “We were tireless because of what was at stake: an economic opportunity that could have been transformative for the county, and for California,” he said. Fortney and other representatives declined to be interviewed for this story, instead sending written responses to CalMatters’ questions. Opponents of California Forever argue that the project’s constant rush for approvals gives project leaders the ability to steamroll public officials. “For something of this size, it’s absurd to push in front of anybody and say, ‘We need your yes vote or your no vote right now,’” said Duane Kromm, a Solano County supervisor between 1999 and 2007 and critic of California Forever. “You wouldn’t buy a used car with that kind of timeframe.” A sign opposing the California Forever development stands on the lawn in front of a Suisun City home on Aug. 4, 2026. Anna Hoch-Kenney/CalMatters Four of the five county supervisors declined to comment on last year’s push by California Forever. Board Chair Monica Brown said she didn’t want to jeopardize her ability to vote on future items related to California Forever, but said little had changed since she addressed the company in 2024 when the company dropped its proposed ballot measure to change the land’s zoning. “This has been stressful not only to those of us up on the dais but (to) our workers,” she says in a video of the remarks. “How dare you come in here with your arrogance. You didn’t even listen. There is a process.” In a statement, county spokesperson Matthew Davis told CalMatters that “while advocacy for project proposals is common, the level and urgency of the advocacy surrounding this legislative proposal were not typical of the county’s experience.” California Forever is now close to getting what it wanted last September. Newsom’s office began circulating a legislative proposal last week that would streamline environmental review of the shipyard development, according to a source directly involved with the negotiations who has reviewed the language. The move comes after weeks of private meetings with California Forever, county leaders and state representatives. But California Forever says the shipyard isn’t enough anymore. It’s now asking the state to help fast-track its proposed advanced manufacturing hub , which could house industries from AI hardware to aerospace and defense, and also expedite building the new city, which the company argues is vital to accommodate the workers the industrial projects would bring. “Since the September 2025 meeting, it has become clear that employers require a broader set of benefits to come to Solano County, including paid-for infrastructure and guarantees of long-term availability of attainable homes. The shipyard alone cannot provide those,” said Jim Wunderman, the company’s head of public affairs and former CEO of the business association Bay Area Council, by email. If a deal does come together, Solano County Administrator Ian Goldberg said he expects county supervisors will be able to weigh in again — next week, in their last meeting before the end of the legislative session. A race against time In late August 2025, state officials learned that Saronic Technologies Inc., a defense start-up with several lucrative U.S. Navy contracts, was planning a visit to Solano County. The company had just picked the county as a finalist for its $3.2 billion shipyard project, but worried that California’s stringent environmental regulations would stall the development. The only solution was special legislation to speed up environmental review for the project before the legislative session wrapped on Sept. 12, Sramek said in an Aug. 29 email to Solano County staff. He wanted the project to rely on a 2008 environmental impact report which designated some of the county’s waterfront for “water-dependent industrial usage,” instead of commissioning a new report for the shipyard, which he said could take up to five years. State law requires those reports for any project that might significantly harm the environment. In recent years, the Legislature has increasingly approved expedited permitting for housing, but not for industrial development. “The fate of 10,000+ jobs is solely in your hands.” California Forever Director of Partnerships Michael Fortney in an email to Solano County staff Over the next two weeks, California Forever representatives mounted a multi-front campaign, including emails, phone calls and texts, to pressure county officials to support legislation. On Sept. 1, 2025, Fortney sent an email to county staff saying they had to decide whether to support the legislative idea that very day. The governor’s office, Sen. Christopher Cabaldon and Assemblymember Lori Wilson , both Democrats who represent the region, and several county supervisors would all be on board if county staff said yes, he said. “We want to be very clear that the fate of 10,000+ jobs is solely in your hands,” Fortney wrote to county staff. But there was no proposal language for staff to evaluate, Bill Emlen, then the county administrator, responded. “This is not the way to make public policy.” Fortney in turn accused county staff of slowwalking the process and presenting “excuse after excuse.” He stressed that the county would be free to approve or deny developments in the shipyard area under the proposal. “We don’t understand why this is complicated for you when it wasn’t complicated for everyone listed above — unless you don’t want these jobs in Solano?” Fortney said. “Staff being the sole party in Solano County that’s delaying this is starting to create serious risk that this is why we run out of time to pass this and lose the opportunity.” Later that night, Fortney again pressed Emlen in an email. “If you fail to timely do so and the county loses the opportunity for a $3bn investment and 10,000+ jobs, even though 27 local leaders and labor have already backed this in the last 3 days, the responsibility will be on you.” On the morning of Sept. 3, 2025, Sramek sent county staff a draft proposal for the first time and announced he would be at the county office in less than three hours to discuss it. County staff should want to meet, he argued, because the revenue from the shipyard alone would single-handedly plug the county’s $44 million budget hole . He accused them of ignoring calls from California Forever and “running out the clock.” Goldberg, then-assistant county administrator, refused to meet. “As you will appreciate, our staff must dedicate time this morning to carefully review and evaluate the language,” Goldberg said in response. Not letting up The same day, Wilson and Cabaldon both declined to introduce legislation, citing the need for more time to flesh out the idea. But California Forever didn’t stop working toward a deal. The group sent out a text poll that day to likely voters, asking them whether the county was heading in the right direction, what their biggest concern was, and whether they would support legislation to allow a new shipyard project, which would “bring billions of dollars of investments and over 10,000 permanent jobs to our county.” The special legislation was needed “to meet national security standards and break ground in 2026.” Fifty-five percent of the 342 poll’s early respondents said yes, about 22% said no, and another 22% were unsure, according to results published in the Fairfield Daily Republic. From left, Planning Commission Chair Albert Enault, Suisun City Mayor Alma Hernandez and Mayor Pro Tem Jenalee Dawson listen to a community member during a council meeting at the Suisun City Hall on Aug. 4, 2026. Anna Hoch-Kenney/CalMatters Following the poll, Fortney emailed at least one county supervisor: “As you’ve seen through the polling, there is overwhelming support for this in Solano County. Nearing 60% of voters here want this, with only about 20% opposed, a margin of 3:1.” In an email to CalMatters last week, Fortney said he continued to push because “when 10,000 jobs are at stake, I think everyone in this community should give 150% until the clock runs out.” On Sept. 8, 2025, county staff finally reached an agreement with California Forever and the governor’s office on a revised draft proposal, even though they told the company’s lobbyist they were “not totally enthused” with the language. That evening, Cabaldon proposed amendments to the legislation that were more favorable to the county. During a board meeting the following day, several county supervisors said they felt rushed into making a decision despite many unaddressed concerns. They reluctantly voted to support the legislation less than two hours after reading it for the first time, with Cabaldon’s last-minute amendments. The final product preserved the county’s ability to require environmental studies and permits for certain areas of the project, Mashburn told fellow supervisors. Ultimately, California Forever deemed the amendments too restrictive. “The legislation as voted on would not have attracted any shipbuilders,” Wunderman said in an email last week. Kromm said the group was “threatening” county officials. “If you don’t do what we want you to do, we are going to blast you publicly about (how) you are not supportive of jobs and the economic health of Solano County,” he said. Princess Washington, a councilmember from Suisun City who opposes that city’s plan to annex California Forever land for development, said rushing can be an effective tactic. “The one rushing the decision has the advantage,” she said. Local governments are divided Urgency is just what Suisun City Manager Bret Prebula believes his city needs. The 4-square-mile city, boxed in by marshes, the city of Fairfield and Travis Air Force Base, has struggled for decades to stay solvent. City leaders have banked on infill projects, state redevelopment funds and sales taxes to raise revenue, but it has always seemed one step from bankruptcy. The only solution, Prebula said, is to expand. So in January 2025, he called California Forever. Suisun City Manager Bret Prebula speaks during a city council meeting at Suisun City Hall on Aug. 4, 2026. Anna Hoch-Kenney/CalMatters The two hatched a bold plan: Let Suisun City annex the company’s more than 22,000 acres of unincorporated county farmland into the city boundaries. The proposal — now going through the process as the Suisun Expansion Plan — would offer California Forever a path to build its projects without requiring approval from skeptical county voters. In turn, California Forever has promised to pay the city $10 million in “public benefits” funding — roughly a third of the city’s annual operating budget, on top of reimbursing the city for costs of exploring the annexation, according to a June 2025 agreement the company signed with the city. The company would pay $3.5 million once the city completes a report assessing the environmental impact of the annexation and another $6.5 million if the annexation is approved. ‘My city is an example of how bureaucracy and politics can stop a city from thriving on its own.’ Suisun City Manager Bret Prebula, who supports California Forever Prebula said the deal would also bring the city millions of dollars in tax revenue if and when the land is developed. But Suisun City could wait years for that due to the state’s strict environmental regulations and the drawn-out annexation process, Prebula said. “My city is an example of how bureaucracy and politics can stop a city from thriving on its own,” he told CalMatters. While Prebula views California Forever as a golden opportunity for his city, leaders in neighboring Rio Vista feel squeezed just half a mile from the eastern border of Suisun City’s proposed expansion. After Suisun City began exploring the annexation, Rio Vista leaders said they felt compelled to make a rival, “last-ditch” pitch — twice — to annex the land themselves, despite concerns about the project’s impact on traffic and the environment, to have some control over the development. In response, California Forever said the city manager was running “ rogue ” and attempting to damage Suisun City’s plans. “Rio Vista is the most impacted city,” Rio Vista Mayor Edwin Okamura told CalMatters. “Yet we don’t have any control over that project. (That) seems ludicrous.” Rio Vista Mayor Edwin Okamura speaks to attendees at the Solano Together/Say No to California Forever reception at Cafeteria 15L in Sacramento on Aug. 5, 2026. Fred Greaves/CalMatters Wunderman dismissed Okamura’s concerns, arguing the company met “dozens of times” with Rio Vista officials, who “have many avenues” to weigh in through the regional annexation process, which allows room for public comment. https://www.politico.eu/article/sweden-e.text: STOCKHOLM — With two days to go before Sweden’s knife-edge general election, Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has a warning for Europe: Don’t trust the left on defense. His country has been almost totally united in its support for Ukraine and in backing the decision — after decades of neutrality — to join NATO two years ago. But speaking to POLITICO in the capital Stockholm, the center-right Moderate party leader argued that Europe should wake up to the security risks of the rival left-wing bloc taking power — which polls suggest may happen. Asked what's at stake for Europe in Sunday’s vote, Kristersson said: “I would say security policy. If the left side would win, two out of three, or two out of four parties voted against the Swedish NATO membership. I mean, that is a real, real thing.” Advertisement Advertisement He continued: “That means a government that will not be able to make the domestic decisions needed to fulfill our NATO obligations, for example — like spending, like all the missions.” Sweden became NATO’s newest member in 2024, the national mood having shifted in favor of taking sides in the face of Vladimir Putin’s territorial aggression in Europe. That decision was “a big thing” for the country of 10.6 million people, which was neutral during both world wars and throughout the Cold War, Kristersson said. “But after becoming a member, we have made a NATO-related decision every month in government,” the prime minister added. “And if government is not united, they simply cannot make the decisions.” Since becoming a member of the alliance, Sweden has sent hundreds of troops to join a NATO force in Latvia, pledged warships for patrolling the Baltic Sea and deployed Gripen fighter jets to police the skies in the region. Asked if he believed support for Ukraine would be in doubt too, Kristersson said: “I hope, really not, because we have been united on Ukraine — with one single exception. The Left Party voted against the very first support package to Ukraine. From that [point] on, eight parties out of eight have been united.” Kristersson’s comments follow a pointed intervention from Social Democrat opposition leader Magdalena Andersson, who demanded the PM come clean about his allies’ links to Russia in a POLITICO interview published this week. Advertisement Advertisement Until recently, Sunday’s upcoming vote seemed like it would be a comfortable victory for Andersson’s Social Democrats and their political allies in smaller parties on the left. But their poll lead shrank dramatically in the past two weeks to as low as 2.6%, within the statistical margin of error. Far-right friends Kristersson’s center-right coalition has been governing for the past four years with the support of the far-right Sweden Democrats. He defended his decision to cooperate with a party opponents claim is too extreme despite its internal efforts to clean up its past neo-Nazi links. “I have full respect for the fact that there are eight parties in the Swedish parliament,” said Kristersson. “None of these parties are even close to a majority of their own. If you cannot unite parties on specific topics and ambitions, then you will simply not get anything done at all.” Under leader Jimmie Åkesson, the Sweden Democrats are in second place behind Andersson’s Social Democrats in the polls. Åkesson has said he’s eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister at the next vote, due in 2030. If Kristersson returns as prime minister after Sunday’s election, he has said he’s ready to give Sweden Democrat politicians roles as ministers in his government for the first time. It would be a major change for Sweden — and the left-wing bloc has campaigned against it. Kristersson suggested that being part of a team would limit the opportunities for any individual ministers to go rogue with extremist policies. “In Sweden, we have a collective decision-making process in government,” he said. “I would never say that one minister is not important, but every minister is part of a team that jointly makes all the decisions — so there is very little room for people to play in a role of their own. “And since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/catego.text: Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the US would continue applying pressure on Iran after what he described as productive discussions with G20 finance ministers. (EPA Images pic) ASHEVILLE: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent vowed Monday to persist with economic pressure on Iran, saying a turning point could be near as G20 finance leaders opened talks clouded by war and trade tensions. "We are going to continue exerting pressure, and we've had very good discussions here already," Bessent told reporters before starting meetings with Group of 20 finance ministers and central bank governors. He said a turning point in this US pressure campaign could come "within weeks or months", adding that Iran's economy need not collapse in the Middle East war to achieve this. President Donald Trump's administration is working to rally G20 partners to ramp up economic pressure on Iran during the talks in Asheville, North Carolina, through Tuesday amid a renewed exchange of fire with Tehran. The first exchange of attacks for a month loomed over the meetings as leaders arrived Monday morning at the foggy, mountainous compound of the Omni Grove Park Inn. Already, the EU urged "continued diplomatic efforts" to reach a peace settlement. It welcomed efforts aimed at ensuring Iran ceases its "destabilising activities and engages in peace negotiations in good faith", including through US-led economic pressure. French finance minister Roland Lescure told reporters that officials would listen to the US plans. "We all need to work on this. The US has got a view on how to enhance sanctions. We're going to discuss with them whether we can help on that front," he said. The G20 comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union. It was established in the wake of the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis to boost global economic and financial stability. 'Ready to discuss' Also weighing on the talks are Trump's trade wars, with observers monitoring if the G-20 can still work together to address big economic challenges. Analysts warn that a US-Canada trade fight impacts unity among the Group of Seven advanced economies as the countries broach tough issues in the wider grouping. G7 finance ministers are also expected to meet on the margins of the Asheville talks. "Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," finance minister Francois-Philippe Champagne told reporters Monday. He stressed the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade, which will benefit all the countries represented here today". Bessent skipped last year's meeting led by South Africa, which has been excluded from the group by the US. Washington holds the rotating presidency this year. Instead, US officials invited Poland to the table, although it is not a permanent G20 member. A Russian representative is participating, too. A European official speaking on condition of anonymity expressed disapproval that Moscow – at war with Ukraine since its 2022 invasion – was not excluded. EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said G7 talks will discuss continuing support for Ukraine, besides the Middle East conflict. Beyond promoting economic growth, US priorities this year include dealing with "global imbalances" and sovereign debt challenges. G20 discussions will seek to ensure that economies avoid policies that push excess production into global markets, a US official said last week. This echoes criticism of China's excess industrial capacity, which critics say drives down prices and causes unfair competition. Certain reporters from major US newsrooms, including The New York Times and Bloomberg News, were not granted credentials to cover the gathering. A Treasury spokesperson said it plans to welcome nearly 300 media representatives from around a dozen countries. All eyes will be on bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the summit too, where Bessent is set to make direct appeals to counterparts as Washington pushes to isolate Iran economically. A Treasury official said Bessent will deliver a strong statement to the G20 to urge compliance with US sanctions. Business leaders, including JPMorgan Chief Executive Jamie Dimon are also present at G20 discussions this year on barriers to investment, innovation and productivity.
